BST260 Final Project Proposal

Yufei Chen

2026-11-18

Source: vignettes/proposal.qmd

To: BST260 Teaching Team, Fall 2026

1. Project Overview

This project will analyze two public health datasets using statistical methods introduced in BST260: NHANES and CDC waterborne illness data. The first analysis will focus on age-specific health outcomes (NHANES Option 1) and incorporate spline regression from Option 2. The second will compare statistical models for outbreak count data. Both analyses will be presented as reproducible Quarto vignettes in the finalproject R package.

2. Analysis 1: NHANES — BMI and Blood Pressure

Research Question

Among U.S. adults aged 40 and older, how is BMI associated with systolic blood pressure, and does spline regression improve model fit compared with linear regression?

Variables and Study Population

  • Population and unit: NHANES participants aged 40+, with each participant representing one observation.
  • Exposure: BMI (kg/m²), modeled continuously and categorized for descriptive analysis.
  • Outcome: Average systolic blood pressure (BPSysAve), a continuous variable measured in mmHg.
  • Confounders: Age, sex, race/ethnicity, and smoking status, selected based on subject-matter considerations.
  • Missing data: Examine missingness and use complete-case analysis as the primary approach.

Planned Statistical Analysis

I will summarize participant characteristics and visualize BMI and blood pressure distributions. Adjusted linear regression will estimate the association between BMI and systolic blood pressure. Natural cubic spline regression using splines::ns() will assess potential nonlinear relationships.

Models will be compared using AIC, fitted curves, and residual diagnostics. I will also explore BMI-by-sex interactions and consider survey weights if suitable design information is available.

3. Analysis 2: CDC Waterborne Illness — Count Regression

Research Question

How does water system type relate to the number of illnesses per reported outbreak, and does negative binomial regression provide a better fit than Poisson regression?

Variables and Study Population

  • Population and unit: Reported U.S. waterborne disease outbreaks, with each outbreak representing one observation.
  • Exposure: Water system type (water_type), comparing community and individual/private systems.
  • Outcome: Number of reported illnesses (illnesses), a nonnegative count variable.
  • Confounders: Calendar period and geographic region, with etiology considered in secondary analyses.
  • Missing data: Convert the list-based dataset into a tidy data frame, examine missing values, and exclude incomplete records from the primary analysis.

Planned Statistical Analysis

I will summarize outbreak frequencies and illness counts by water system type, region, and year. Visualizations will include distributions of outbreak sizes and temporal trends.

I will fit Poisson and negative binomial regression models and compare AIC, dispersion statistics, residual diagnostics, and estimated associations. Sensitivity analyses will assess the influence of unusually large outbreaks.

4. Reproducibility and Limitations

The project will include two analysis vignettes:

  • nhanes_analysis.qmd: BMI and systolic blood pressure using linear and spline regression.
  • waterborne_analysis.qmd: Waterborne outbreak counts using Poisson and negative binomial regression.

Both analyses will document data provenance, descriptive statistics, visualizations, reusable R functions, statistical findings, and limitations.

Potential limitations include missing data, residual confounding, NHANES survey design, and incomplete outbreak reporting. Results will be interpreted as observational associations rather than causal effects.

The completed project will be published through the finalproject pkgdown website on GitHub Pages.
